roadmap.lecture_goal: understand the principles, cycles, and techniques required for effective XR system implementation.

objectives.text: You'll be able to summarize the scope of XR system implementation and its foundational concepts.
You'll be able to explain the necessity of iterative development cycles and differentiate between horizontal and vertical prototyping approaches.
You'll be able to apply various prototyping techniques, including low-fidelity design, storyboarding, and the Wizard of Oz method, to visualize complex user interactions.

segments.subgoal: Summarize prior learning and introduce the concept of XR system implementation

key_points.text: The course has previously covered two main areas: gathering user requirements and designing the experience.
Requirement gathering involved learning various techniques, such as data collection and analysis.
Design discussions focused specifically on interface and interaction, rather than standard code or system design.
The current lecture segment introduces the final phase of the system development process: implementation.

key_terms.definition: User requirement gathering is the process of determining what a user needs from a system, which involves utilizing various data collection and analysis techniques. This process was applied to the Majuli Island virtual tour design case study.
Designing the experience is the process of creating the overall user experience based on the requirements that were gathered. This stage follows the requirement gathering phase.

Interface and interaction refers to the specific design focus area that was discussed, dealing with how the user interacts with the system. This focus was maintained because the design approaches for code and system design were considered standard.

segments.subgoal: Describe the iterative cycles used in developing interactive system prototypes and evaluating them

key_points.text: The core development cycle involves design, prototyping, quick evaluation, and subsequent design refinement.
Standard software development includes code design, coding, and code testing stages.
Empirical or usability evaluation occurs after code testing and can lead to returning to the design or interface stage.
This lecture focuses on concepts like prototyping and usability evaluation, rather than code-related implementations.

key_terms.definition: Empirical or usability evaluation is the process of evaluating the whole system from the point of view of usability. This evaluation occurs after the code testing is complete.

Interactive system development lifecycle is a framework equally applicable for extended reality systems. This lifecycle begins with a feasibility study stage, followed by requirement gathering analysis and specification stage.
Design prototype evaluate cycle is a connected sequence of stages. This cycle includes the design stage, prototype stage, and early evaluation or quick evaluation stage.

System implementation refers to the overall process of realizing design ideas that have been formulated based on requirements. This scope is distinct from code-related implementations, which are not the primary focus of this lecture.

segments.subgoal: Explain the necessity and requirements of quick design-prototype-evaluate cycles

key_points.text: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle involves designing, quickly prototyping, evaluating, finding problems, refining, and repeating the process.
To manage frequent design cycles without cost overrun, a quick usability evaluation technique is required.
Quick evaluation requires two components: a prototype (a quickly built model) and the ability to test that prototype quickly.
The lecture will focus on prototyping and early/final usability evaluation, rather than code evaluation.

key_terms.definition: Design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the entire process of creating an immersive experience, which involves designing, quickly prototyping, and then evaluating the design. This cycle is iterative, requiring refinement and new prototypes until the design is stabilized.

Usability evaluation is the process of testing design ideas to determine if they will lead to a usable system once implemented. This evaluation must be conducted quickly to prevent increased turnaround time and cost overrun.
A prototype is a model of an idea that must be built quickly. This model allows for the demonstration of the idea before the system is fully implemented.

segments.subgoal: Explain the purpose and lifecycle of prototypes in system development

key_points.text: Full implementation of a software idea is costly and risks wasting time if the idea is not good.
Prototypes are lightweight implementations used to test a design idea with significantly fewer resources than a full implementation.
Prototypes can be utilized either by being discarded after testing or by being incrementally refined into the final product.

key_terms.definition: Prototype is a lightweight implementation used to test a design idea in practice. Prototypes require significantly fewer resources, skilled manpower, and cost compared to a full implementation.

segments.subgoal: Compare the characteristics and purposes of horizontal and vertical prototypes

key_points.text: Horizontal prototypes depict the entire interface at a surface level without providing any functionality, focusing only on appearance.,
Horizontal prototypes are suitable for brainstorming and eliciting feedback on the interface's look, feel, and usability.,
Vertical prototypes are designed to represent interactions and functionalities by implementing selected features in depth.,
In summary, horizontal prototypes prototype appearances, while vertical prototypes primarily prototype interactions.,

key_terms.definition: Horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level without providing any functionality. Horizontal prototypes primarily prototype the look and feel and appearance of the interface, rather than how a user interacts with it.

Vertical prototype is a prototype designed to represent interactions and functionalities, rather than just the appearance. Vertical prototypes implement selected features in depth, starting from the first screen through the last action performed.

segments.subgoal: Describe the characteristics and application of low-fidelity prototyping

key_points.text: Low-fidelity prototypes are created without requiring technological intervention, code, or computers, often using materials like paper or cardboard.
Low-fidelity prototypes are beneficial because they provide a quick and cheap way to brainstorm designs and gather user feedback on usability.
Interface sketches are drawings that depict major components of an interface to help envision its appearance.
Sketches are primarily used for horizontal prototypes because they do not convey the sequence of actions or interactions required to execute a task.

key_terms.definition: Low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, meaning no programming or computer is required. These prototypes are typically constructed using simple materials like paper, cardboard, or wood.

Interface sketch is a drawing that depicts major components of an interface and provides a simple illustration to envision the appearance of the interface. Interface sketches allow an idea to be expressed so that others or users can comment on it or provide feedback.

Horizontal prototyping is primarily used to represent interface ideas and brainstorm alternative designs, allowing users to provide feedback on the overall concept and usability. This approach focuses on depicting the major components and appearance of the interface but does not detail the sequence of actions or the corresponding changes needed to execute a task.

segments.subgoal: Apply storyboarding techniques to visualize and capture complex user interactions

key_points.text: Storyboarding uses a series of sketches to create a vertical prototype that depicts user interaction, unlike a single sketch which creates a horizontal prototype.
Each sketch within a storyboard is a keyframe, representing a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time.
The overall purpose of a prototype is to follow an iterative cycle: generate an idea, create a prototype, evaluate it, and revise it if issues are found.
A storyboard captures the complete sequence of actions required from the user to achieve a specific task, showing both the user's actions and the corresponding screens.

key_terms.definition: Storyboarding is a series of sketches used to represent interaction. Storyboarding captures the sequence of actions required from the user to complete a specific task.
Keyframe is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time. Each keyframe shows a specific instance of how the screen appears to the user during the execution of a task.
Horizontal prototype is a representation created using a single sketch. A series of sketches, conversely, allows for a vertical prototype that depicts interaction.

Vertical prototype is a representation created using a series of sketches, often called storyboarding. This approach is used to depict the interaction flow of a system, distinguishing it from a horizontal prototype which uses only a single sketch.

segments.subgoal: Compare and contrast low, medium, and high fidelity prototyping approaches

key_points.text: Low fidelity prototypes are typically paper-based and do not require the use of computers.
Medium fidelity prototypes use computers to create simple prototypes, which can include videos or simulated interactions.
